claims.text: Pack-cementation aluminizing enriches the refractory high-entropy alloy surface with aluminum.
Surface aluminizing will produce a continuous alumina layer on the alloy.
The alumina layer produced by aluminizing will adhere to the alloy.
The alumina layer will decrease high-temperature oxygen uptake relative to the untreated alloy.
The untreated refractory high-entropy alloy exhibits rapid oxidation under extreme-temperature conditions.
The untreated alloy exhibits oxide-scale degradation under extreme-temperature conditions.
At high temperature, aluminum deposited at the surface reacts with oxygen to form alumina.
The resulting alumina is a slow-growing and stable barrier.
The alumina barrier impedes further oxygen diffusion into the alloy.
Impeded oxygen diffusion reduces the alloy's oxidation rate.
The alumina barrier prevents catastrophic oxide-scale spallation.
After 100 hours in air at approximately 1100°C, aluminized samples will have around 30% less oxidation mass gain than untreated samples.
After the specified exposure, aluminized samples will have better oxide-scale integrity and minimal spallation relative to untreated samples.
Under the same exposure conditions, the untreated alloy develops a less protective oxide scale.
The less protective scale on the untreated alloy leads to higher oxygen uptake.
The less protective scale on the untreated alloy leads to detrimental microstructural degradation.
The protective effect may not persist under more aggressive thermal cycling or in different atmospheric compositions.
The magnitude of oxidation reduction may depend on alloy composition, aluminizing parameters, and microstructure.
